title: Rational Functions of the Form f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d)
overview: When both the numerator and the denominator are linear, the graph keeps the two-branch shape of $\frac{1}{x}$ but its horizontal asymptote can be any height. These functions describe real ratios – concentrations, average costs, percentages – and you can read every key feature straight from the coefficients.
objectives: Find the vertical and horizontal asymptotes of $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$.
Find the intercepts, domain and range.
Describe the behaviour near the vertical asymptote and the end behaviour.
Compare functions and explain the role of each coefficient.
Write an equation from given key features or a graph.
Model and solve problems involving ratios such as concentrations and average cost.

lessons.title: Linear over linear
lessons.body:
Now both the numerator and the denominator are linear:

$$f(x) = \frac{ax + b}{cx + d}$$

These functions model **ratios that change over time** – a concentration, an average cost, a percentage. Each key feature comes from a different part of the formula:

| Feature | Where it comes from | Result |
|---|---|---|
| vertical asymptote | denominator $= 0$ (numerator not also 0) | $x = -\dfrac{d}{c}$ |
| horizontal asymptote | behaviour for huge $x$ | $y = \dfrac{a}{c}$ |
| $x$-intercept | numerator $= 0$ | $x = -\dfrac{b}{a}$ |
| $y$-intercept | $f(0)$ | $y = \dfrac{b}{d}$ |

**Example:** $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x - 2}$: vertical asymptote $x = 2$, horizontal asymptote $y = 1$, $x$-intercept $-3$, $y$-intercept $-1.5$.

```plot
title: f(x) = (x + 3)/(x − 2)
f: (x+3)/(x-2)
domain: -8, 10
range: -6, 8
points: (-3,0), (0,-1.5)
asymptote x: 2
asymptote y: 1
```

lessons.title: Finding the horizontal asymptote: divide by x
lessons.body:
Why is the horizontal asymptote $y = \frac{a}{c}$? **Divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x$:**

$$f(x) = \frac{ax + b}{cx + d} = \frac{a + \frac{b}{x}}{c + \frac{d}{x}}$$

As $x \to \pm\infty$, the terms $\frac{b}{x}$ and $\frac{d}{x}$ shrink to 0, leaving $\frac{a}{c}$.

**Example:** $g(x) = \dfrac{4x - 7}{2x + 1} = \dfrac{4 - \frac{7}{x}}{2 + \frac{1}{x}} \to \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$. Horizontal asymptote $y = 2$.

**Which side does it approach from?** Test a large value: $g(1000) = \frac{3993}{2001} = 1.9955$ – just **below** 2. And $g(-1000) = \frac{-4007}{-1999} = 2.0045$ – just **above** 2.

> In plain words: for huge $x$, the "+b" and "+d" are tiny compared with $ax$ and $cx$, so $f(x) \approx \frac{ax}{cx} = \frac{a}{c}$.

lessons.title: The vertical asymptote – and the special case of a hole
lessons.body:
Set the denominator to zero: $cx + d = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\frac{d}{c}$.

**But check the numerator!** If the numerator is also zero at that $x$, the factor cancels and there is no asymptote. For example

$$\frac{2x - 6}{x - 3} = \frac{2(x - 3)}{x - 3} = 2, \quad x \ne 3$$

is just the horizontal line $y = 2$ with a single missing point (a **hole**) at $(3, 2)$. You will meet holes again in Section 3.5.

### Behaviour near the vertical asymptote
Test values on each side. For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x - 2}$: $f(1.99) = \frac{4.99}{-0.01} = -499$ and $f(2.01) = \frac{5.01}{0.01} = 501$. So $f(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to 2^-$ and $f(x) \to +\infty$ as $x \to 2^+$.

lessons.title: Symmetry, slope and the role of each coefficient
lessons.body:
The two branches are **equidistant from the point where the asymptotes cross** – the graph has half-turn symmetry about that point.

**Slope:** on each branch the function is either increasing or decreasing everywhere. Test one point on each side to find out which. For $\frac{x+3}{x-2}$ both branches are decreasing.

**Rewriting as a transformation of $\frac{1}{x}$.** Divide (or rearrange) the numerator:

$$\frac{2x + 3}{x + 1} = \frac{2(x + 1) + 1}{x + 1} = 2 + \frac{1}{x + 1}$$

This is $y = \frac{1}{x}$ translated 1 unit left and 2 units up: asymptotes $x = -1$ and $y = 2$.

### Comparing functions
| Function | Vertical asymptote | Horizontal asymptote | $x$-int | $y$-int |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$ | $x = 3$ | $y = 2$ | $-0.5$ | $-\frac{1}{3}$ |
| $\dfrac{2x + 5}{x - 3}$ | $x = 3$ | $y = 2$ | $-2.5$ | $-\frac{5}{3}$ |

Changing $b$ changes the intercepts and how "stretched" the curve is, but **not** the asymptotes, domain or range. Changing $d$ shifts the vertical asymptote.

```plot
f: (2*x+1)/(x-3) | label=(2x + 1)/(x − 3)
f: (2*x+5)/(x-3) | dashed; label=(2x + 5)/(x − 3)
domain: -8, 12
range: -8, 12
asymptote x: 3
asymptote y: 2
```

lessons.title: Writing equations from key features
lessons.body:
Work backwards from the table of features.

**Example:** find $f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}$ with $x$-intercept $-4$, vertical asymptote $x = 2$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 1$.

* $x$-intercept $-4$ → numerator has the factor $(x + 4)$.
* vertical asymptote $x = 2$ → denominator has the factor $(x - 2)$.
* horizontal asymptote $y = 1$ → leading coefficients in the ratio $\frac{a}{c} = 1$.

$$f(x) = \frac{x + 4}{x - 2}$$

Check the $y$-intercept: $f(0) = \frac{4}{-2} = -2$. If the question also gave a $y$-intercept, this is how you verify it.

In general, if the $x$-intercept is $p$, the vertical asymptote $x = q$ and the horizontal asymptote $y = r$, then

$$f(x) = \frac{r(x - p)}{x - q}$$

lessons.title: Applications: concentrations and averages
lessons.body:
Linear-over-linear functions describe how a **ratio** changes.

**Pollutant concentration.** A pond holds 5000 L of clean water. Water carrying 20 g/L of pollutant flows in at 10 L/min. After $t$ minutes the amount of pollutant is $200t$ g and the volume is $5000 + 10t$ L, so

$$C(t) = \frac{200t}{5000 + 10t} \text{ g/L}$$

The horizontal asymptote $C = \frac{200}{10} = 20$ means the concentration approaches the concentration of the incoming water but never quite reaches it.

```plot
title: C(t) = 200t/(5000 + 10t), t in minutes
f: 200*x/(5000+10*x)
domain: 0, 3000
range: 0, 22
asymptote y: 20
ticks: 500, 5
```

**Average cost.** If making $x$ items costs a fixed amount $F$ dollars plus $v$ dollars per item, the average cost per item is $A(x) = \dfrac{vx + F}{x}$, which approaches $v$ as production grows.

keyTerms.definition: The value the function approaches as x → ±∞, found by dividing every term by x.
A single missing point on a graph, caused by a factor that cancels from the numerator and denominator.
The intersection of the vertical and horizontal asymptotes; the two branches are equidistant from it.
What the function does as $x \to \pm\infty$, including whether it approaches the horizontal asymptote from above or below.

formulas.name: Vertical asymptote
formulas.meaning: Provided the numerator is not also zero there.

formulas.name: Equation from features
formulas.meaning: x-intercept p, vertical asymptote x = q, horizontal asymptote y = r.

workedExamples.title: Determine key features
workedExamples.problem: Determine the key features of $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x - 2}$ and describe the graph.
steps: **Vertical asymptote:** $x - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2$ (the numerator is $5 \ne 0$ there). Domain $\{x \mid x \ne 2\}$.
**Horizontal asymptote:** divide by $x$: $\frac{1 + 3/x}{1 - 2/x} \to 1$, so $y = 1$. Range $\{y \mid y \ne 1\}$.
**Slope:** test points show the function is decreasing on both branches.
workedExamples.answer: Asymptotes $x = 2$, $y = 1$; intercepts $(-3, 0)$ and $(0, -1.5)$; decreasing on both intervals.

workedExamples.title: Compare rational functions
steps: Both have vertical asymptote $x = 3$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 2$; same domain and range.
Rewrite: $f = 2 + \frac{7}{x-3}$ and $g = 2 + \frac{11}{x - 3}$, so $g$ is a larger vertical stretch of $\frac{1}{x-3}$ about $y = 2$.
workedExamples.answer: Same asymptotes, domain and range; different intercepts and stretch.

workedExamples.title: Write an equation from features
workedExamples.problem: Write $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ with $x$-intercept 3, vertical asymptote $x = -2$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 2$. State the $y$-intercept.
steps: Horizontal asymptote $\frac{a}{c} = 2$, so multiply the numerator by 2: $f(x) = \dfrac{2(x - 3)}{x + 2} = \dfrac{2x - 6}{x + 2}$.

workedExamples.title: Rewrite as a transformation
steps: Start with $y = \frac{1}{x}$, translate 1 left and 2 up.
workedExamples.answer: $p(x) = 2 + \dfrac{1}{x+1}$: decreasing on both branches, centre of symmetry $(-1, 2)$.

workedExamples.title: Concentration model
workedExamples.problem: $C(t) = \dfrac{200t}{5000 + 10t}$ g/L. When does the concentration reach 10 g/L?

misconceptions.fact: It is the **ratio** of the leading coefficients: $y = \frac{4}{2} = 2$.
$x$-intercepts come from the **numerator**; the denominator gives the vertical asymptote.

misconceptions.myth: Every zero of the denominator gives a vertical asymptote.
misconceptions.fact: Only if the numerator is not also zero there; a common factor gives a **hole** instead.

misconceptions.myth: The graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote, so $y = \frac{a}{c}$ is excluded from the range.
misconceptions.fact: For linear-over-linear functions it is true that $\frac{a}{c}$ is never reached, but the reason is algebra (solving $f(x) = \frac{a}{c}$ has no solution), not a rule about asymptotes in general.

misconceptions.myth: Changing the constant $b$ in the numerator moves the asymptotes.
misconceptions.fact: $b$ changes the intercepts and the stretch only; $c$ and $d$ fix the vertical asymptote, and $\frac{a}{c}$ fixes the horizontal one.

realWorld.title: Environmental clean-up
realWorld.body: Concentration models like $C(t) = \frac{200t}{5000+10t}$ help engineers predict how polluted a pond or lake will become after a spill, and how long that will take.

realWorld.title: Business
realWorld.body: Average cost per item, $\frac{vx + F}{x}$, falls toward the variable cost $v$ as production grows – the reason large factories can sell more cheaply.

realWorld.title: Mixing solutions
realWorld.body: Adding $x$ L of pure acid to 10 L of 20% acid gives concentration $\frac{2 + x}{10 + x}$, which approaches 100% but never reaches it.

realWorld.title: Sports statistics
realWorld.body: A batting average after $x$ more hits in $x$ more at-bats, $\frac{h + x}{n + x}$, creeps toward 1.000 – a linear-over-linear function.

practice.question: Find the vertical asymptote and domain of $f(x) = \dfrac{3x}{x - 7}$.
Find the horizontal asymptote and range of $p(x) = \dfrac{5x + 1}{x - 6}$.
Describe the end behaviour of $g(x) = \dfrac{3 - x}{2 + x}$.
practice.hint: Divide by $x$ and test large values.
practice.solution: $\frac{3/x - 1}{2/x + 1} \to -1$. $g(1000) = -0.995$ (above −1), $g(-1000) = -1.005$ (below −1). So $y \to -1$ from above as $x \to \infty$ and from below as $x \to -\infty$.

practice.question: Write an equation for a rational function with $x$-intercept $-4$, $y$-intercept $-2$ and vertical asymptote $x = 2$.
For $k(x) = \dfrac{6x + 2}{2x - 1}$ list the asymptotes and intercepts.

summary: For $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$: vertical asymptote $x = -\frac{d}{c}$ (if the numerator is not also zero there), horizontal asymptote $y = \frac{a}{c}$.
Find the horizontal asymptote by dividing every term by $x$ and letting $x \to \pm\infty$.
The coefficient $b$ stretches the curve but does not change the asymptotes, domain or range; $d$ shifts the vertical asymptote.
The two branches are equidistant from the intersection of the asymptotes.
Linear-over-linear functions model concentrations, averages and percentages.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{c}}x - {{d}} = 0 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{ {{d}} }{ {{c}} } \approx {{d/c:3}}$. (The numerator is not zero there.)

(b) Dividing by $x$: $\dfrac{ {{a}} + \frac{ {{b}} }{x} }{ {{c}} - \frac{ {{d}} }{x} } \to \dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{c}} }$, so $y \approx {{a/c:3}}$.

(c) $x$-intercept: ${{a}}x + {{b}} = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\dfrac{ {{b}} }{ {{a}} } \approx {{-b/a:3}}$.

(d) $y$-intercept: $f(0) = \dfrac{ {{b}} }{-{{d}}} \approx {{-b/d:3}}$.

Domain $\{x \mid x \ne {{d/c:3}}\}$, range $\{y \mid y \ne {{a/c:3}}\}$.

questions.text: Explain, by dividing each term by $x$, why the horizontal asymptote of $g(x) = \dfrac{ {{a}}x - {{b}} }{ {{c}}x + {{d}} }$ is $y = \dfrac{ {{a}} }{ {{c}} }$. Then determine whether the graph approaches the asymptote from above or below as $x \to +\infty$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the reasoning and the direction of approach.

questions.modelAnswer:
$g(x) = \dfrac{ {{a}} - \frac{ {{b}} }{x} }{ {{c}} + \frac{ {{d}} }{x} }$. As $x \to \pm\infty$ the fractions $\frac{ {{b}} }{x}$ and $\frac{ {{d}} }{x}$ approach 0, so $g(x) \to \frac{ {{a}} }{ {{c}} } \approx {{a/c:3}}$.

At $x = 1000$: $g(1000) = \dfrac{ {{1000*a-b}} }{ {{1000*c+d}} } \approx {{(1000*a-b)/(1000*c+d):5}}$, which is **less** than {{a/c:4}}, so the graph approaches from **below** as $x \to +\infty$.

rubric.point: Divides each term by x correctly
Explains terms with x in the denominator → 0
Tests a large value and concludes direction correctly

questions.text: Write an equation of the form $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ whose graph has an $x$-intercept of {{p}}, a vertical asymptote $x = -{{q}}$ and a horizontal asymptote $y = {{r}}$. Then find the $y$-intercept and check all features.
questions.modelAnswer:
$x$-intercept {{p}} → numerator factor $(x - {{p}})$. Vertical asymptote $x = -{{q}}$ → denominator $(x + {{q}})$. Horizontal asymptote $y = {{r}}$ → ratio of leading coefficients {{r}}.

$f(x) = \dfrac{ {{r}}(x - {{p}}) }{x + {{q}}} = \dfrac{ {{r}}x - {{r*p}} }{x + {{q}}}$.

$y$-intercept $f(0) = \dfrac{-{{r*p}}}{ {{q}} } \approx {{-r*p/q:3}}$.

Check: $f({{p}}) = 0$ ✓; denominator zero at $x = -{{q}}$ and numerator $\ne 0$ there ✓; $\frac{ {{r}} }{1} = {{r}}$ ✓.

questions.text: For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + {{b}}}{x - {{d}}}$, determine the intervals on which the function is positive and negative, and whether it is increasing or decreasing on each branch. Use test points.
questions.modelAnswer:
Key values: $x = -{{b}}$ (zero) and $x = {{d}}$ (vertical asymptote).

| Interval | $x < -{{b}}$ | $-{{b}} < x < {{d}}$ | $x > {{d}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| test | $x = {{-b-1}}$ | $x = 0$ | $x = {{d+1}}$ |
| sign | + | − | + |

Slope: $f({{d+1}}) = {{(d+1+b)/1:3}}$ and $f({{d+2}}) = {{(d+2+b)/2:3}}$ – decreasing on the right branch. On the left, $f(-100) \approx {{(-100+b)/(-100-d):4}}$ and $f(-10) \approx {{(-10+b)/(-10-d):4}}$ – also decreasing (values fall toward −∞ as $x \to {{d}}^-$). The function is **decreasing on both branches**.

rubric.point: Correct sign on each interval with test points
Determines slope on both branches with evidence

questions.text: Compare $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{a}}x + 1}{x - {{d}}}$ and $g(x) = \dfrac{ {{a}}x + {{b2}} }{x - {{d}}}$. Describe their similarities and differences, and explain the role of the constant in the numerator.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Same:** vertical asymptote $x = {{d}}$, horizontal asymptote $y = {{a}}$, domain $x \ne {{d}}$, range $y \ne {{a}}$, general shape (two branches on opposite corners of the asymptotes).

**Different:** $x$-intercepts $-\frac{1}{ {{a}} } \approx {{-1/a:3}}$ and $-\frac{ {{b2}} }{ {{a}} } \approx {{-b2/a:3}}$; $y$-intercepts $-\frac{1}{ {{d}} } \approx {{-1/d:3}}$ and $-\frac{ {{b2}} }{ {{d}} } \approx {{-b2/d:3}}$.

Rewriting: $f = {{a}} + \dfrac{ {{a*d+1}} }{x - {{d}}}$ and $g = {{a}} + \dfrac{ {{a*d+b2}} }{x - {{d}}}$, so the constant in the numerator acts like a vertical stretch about the asymptote; it does not affect the asymptotes, domain or range.

rubric.point: Explains the constant as a stretch with no effect on asymptotes

questions.text: After a spill, the concentration of a pollutant in a pond is modelled by $C(t) = \dfrac{ {{a}}t}{ {{b}} + t}$ grams per litre, where $t$ is the time in minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What concentration does the model approach in the long run?

parts.label: c
parts.text: When does the concentration reach {{a/2}} g/L?

parts.label: d
parts.text: State a suitable domain and range and comment on the vertical asymptote.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) As $t \to \infty$, $C(t) = \dfrac{ {{a}} }{\frac{ {{b}} }{t} + 1} \to {{a}}$. The concentration approaches {{a}} g/L in the long run but never reaches it.

(b) $C({{t1}}) = \dfrac{ {{a}}({{t1}}) }{ {{b}} + {{t1}} } \approx {{a*t1/(b+t1):3}}$ g/L.

(c) $\dfrac{ {{a}}t}{ {{b}} + t} = {{a/2}}$ gives ${{a}}t = {{a/2}}({{b}} + t)$, so ${{a/2}}t = {{a*b/2}}$ and $t = {{b}}$ min.

(d) Domain $t \ge 0$, range $0 \le C < {{a}}$. The vertical asymptote $t = -{{b}}$ is outside the domain and has no meaning here.

questions.text:
The graph shows a function of the form $f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{x + d}$ with its asymptotes and $x$-intercept marked.

```plot
f: {{r}}*(x-{{p}})/(x+{{q}})
domain: -12, 12
range: -12, 16
points: ({{p}},0)
asymptote x: -{{q}}
asymptote y: {{r}}
```

The marked $x$-intercept is $({{p}}, 0)$, the vertical asymptote is $x = -{{q}}$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y = {{r}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the $y$-intercept to check your equation.

questions.modelAnswer:
From the graph: vertical asymptote $x = -{{q}}$ → denominator $x + {{q}}$; horizontal asymptote $y = {{r}}$ → $a = {{r}}$; $x$-intercept {{p}} → numerator $ {{r}}(x - {{p}})$.

$f(x) = \dfrac{ {{r}}x - {{r*p}} }{x + {{q}}}$, so $a = {{r}}$, $b = -{{r*p}}$, $d = {{q}}$.

Check: $y$-intercept $f(0) = -\frac{ {{r*p}} }{ {{q}} } \approx {{-r*p/q:3}}$, consistent with the graph crossing the $y$-axis below the origin.

rubric.point: Reads horizontal asymptote and links to a

questions.text: Rewrite $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{a}}x + {{b}} }{x + {{d}}}$ in the form $f(x) = {{a}} + \dfrac{k}{x + {{d}}}$. Use this form to describe the transformations of $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$, and explain why the two branches are equidistant from the point where the asymptotes meet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the transformations and explain the symmetry.

questions.modelAnswer:
${{a}}x + {{b}} = {{a}}(x + {{d}}) + ({{b}} - {{a*d}})$, so

$f(x) = {{a}} + \dfrac{ {{b-a*d}} }{x + {{d}}}$, i.e. $k = {{b-a*d}}$.

Transformations of $y = \frac{1}{x}$: vertical stretch by a factor of $|{{b-a*d}}|$ (with a reflection in the $x$-axis if $k < 0$), translation {{d}} units left and {{a}} units up.

Since $y = \frac{1}{x}$ is symmetric about the origin (a half-turn about $(0,0)$ maps the graph to itself), its image is symmetric about the image of the origin, $(-{{d}}, {{a}})$ – exactly where the asymptotes $x = -{{d}}$ and $y = {{a}}$ intersect.

rubric.point: Explains symmetry about intersection of asymptotes

questions.text: Explain why $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{k}}x - {{k*h}} }{x - {{h}}}$ does not have a vertical asymptote at $x = {{h}}$, even though the denominator is zero there. Describe its graph.
questions.modelAnswer:
Factor the numerator: ${{k}}x - {{k*h}} = {{k}}(x - {{h}})$. So $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{k}}(x - {{h}}) }{x - {{h}}} = {{k}}$ for $x \ne {{h}}$.

At $x = {{h}}$ both the numerator and the denominator are 0, so the function is undefined, but the values near $x = {{h}}$ are all equal to {{k}} – they do not grow without bound. The graph is the horizontal line $y = {{k}}$ with a **hole** at $({{h}}, {{k}})$, not an asymptote.

rubric.point: Explains values stay finite near x = h
Describes the line with a hole at the correct point

questions.text: For $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{a}}x - 1}{x + {{d}}}$, state the domain and range in set notation. Show algebraically that $f(x)$ can never equal {{a}}.
questions.modelAnswer:
Domain $\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid x \ne -{{d}}\}$, range $\{y \in \mathbb{R} \mid y \ne {{a}}\}$.

Suppose $\dfrac{ {{a}}x - 1}{x + {{d}}} = {{a}}$. Then ${{a}}x - 1 = {{a}}x + {{a*d}}$, so $-1 = {{a*d}}$, which is false. No $x$ gives $f(x) = {{a}}$, confirming that $y = {{a}}$ is excluded from the range (it is the horizontal asymptote).

questions.text: Estimate the instantaneous rate of change of $f(x) = \dfrac{x - {{p}}}{x + {{q}}}$ at its $x$-intercept, using a secant from $x = {{p}}$ to $x = {{p}}.001$.
questions.modelAnswer:
$x$-intercept: $x = {{p}}$, so $f({{p}}) = 0$.

$f({{p}}.001) = \dfrac{0.001}{ {{p+q}}.001} \approx {{0.001/(p+q+0.001):4}}$.

Rate $\approx \dfrac{ {{0.001/(p+q+0.001):4}} - 0}{0.001} \approx {{1/(p+q):3}}$.

Positive: the function is increasing as it crosses the $x$-axis.

questions.text: Describe the end behaviour of $h(x) = \dfrac{ {{b}} - x}{ {{d}} + x}$ as $x \to +\infty$ and as $x \to -\infty$, including whether the graph approaches its horizontal asymptote from above or below. Support your answer with calculations.
questions.modelAnswer:
Divide by $x$: $h(x) = \dfrac{\frac{ {{b}} }{x} - 1}{\frac{ {{d}} }{x} + 1} \to -1$. Horizontal asymptote $y = -1$.

$h(1000) = \dfrac{ {{b-1000}} }{ {{d+1000}} } \approx {{(b-1000)/(d+1000):5}}$, which is **above** −1, so $h \to -1^+$ (from above) as $x \to +\infty$.

$h(-1000) = \dfrac{ {{b+1000}} }{ {{d-1000}} } \approx {{(b+1000)/(d-1000):5}}$, which is **below** −1, so $h \to -1$ from below as $x \to -\infty$.

rubric.point: Correct calculation at a large positive x
Correct calculation at a large negative x

questions.text: A company's cost to produce $x$ custom jackets is {{F}} dollars in set-up costs plus {{v}} dollars per jacket. The average cost per jacket is $A(x) = \dfrac{ {{v}}x + {{F}} }{x}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the average cost for {{x1}} jackets.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many jackets must be made for the average cost to be at most {{T}} dollars?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $A({{x1}}) = \dfrac{ {{v}}({{x1}}) + {{F}} }{ {{x1}} } \approx {{(v*x1+F)/x1:4}}$ dollars.

(b) As $x \to \infty$, $A(x) = {{v}} + \frac{ {{F}} }{x} \to {{v}}$: horizontal asymptote $A = {{v}}$. The average cost approaches the cost of materials per jacket because the set-up cost is shared among more and more jackets.

(c) ${{v}} + \dfrac{ {{F}} }{x} \le {{T}}$ gives $\dfrac{ {{F}} }{x} \le {{T-v}}$, so $x \ge \dfrac{ {{F}} }{ {{T-v}} } \approx {{F/(T-v):4}}$. At least {{ceil(F/(T-v))}} jackets are needed.

(d) The vertical asymptote $x = 0$ means the average cost becomes huge for very small orders.

questions.text: Describe the roles of the numerator and the denominator in determining the key features of the graph of $f(x) = \dfrac{ax+b}{cx+d}$.
questions.modelAnswer:
* **Denominator:** its zero, $x = -\frac{d}{c}$, gives the vertical asymptote (and so the domain restriction), unless the numerator is also zero there (then there is a hole). The constant $d$ shifts the vertical asymptote.
* **Numerator:** its zero, $x = -\frac{b}{a}$, gives the $x$-intercept. The constant $b$ acts like a stretch and changes the intercepts but not the asymptotes.
* **Both together:** the ratio of the leading coefficients $\frac{a}{c}$ gives the horizontal asymptote (and the excluded value in the range); the ratio of the constants $\frac{b}{d}$ gives the $y$-intercept.

rubric.point: Constant ratio → y-intercept; role of b and d

questions.text: Summarize all key features of $k(x) = \dfrac{6x + 2}{2x - 1}$ (asymptotes, intercepts, domain, range, behaviour near the vertical asymptote, end behaviour and intervals of increase or decrease), then describe its graph.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the remaining features and the graph.

questions.modelAnswer:
Vertical asymptote $2x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0.5$; horizontal asymptote $y = \frac{6}{2} = 3$.

$x$-intercept $6x + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\frac{1}{3}$; $y$-intercept $k(0) = -2$.

Domain $x \ne 0.5$, range $y \ne 3$.

Near $x = 0.5$: $k(0.49) = \frac{4.94}{-0.02} = -247$, $k(0.51) = \frac{5.06}{0.02} = 253$: $k \to -\infty$ as $x \to 0.5^-$ and $k \to +\infty$ as $x \to 0.5^+$.

End behaviour: $k(1000) \approx 3.005$ (above 3), $k(-1000) \approx 2.995$ (below 3).

Rewriting: $k(x) = 3 + \frac{5}{2x - 1}$, so the function is decreasing on both branches. The branches lie in the top-right and bottom-left regions formed by the asymptotes, symmetric about $(0.5, 3)$.

rubric.point: Decreasing on both branches with evidence

questions.text: A chemist has 10 L of a solution that is {{p0}}% acid. She adds $x$ litres of pure acid. The concentration of the mixture is $C(x) = \dfrac{ {{p0/10}} + x}{10 + x}$ (as a decimal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the model is correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How much pure acid gives a {{T}}% solution?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Acid: ${{p0/10}}$ L in 10 L. After adding $x$ L of pure acid: acid ${{p0/10}} + x$, volume $10 + x$, so $C(x) = \frac{ {{p0/10}} + x}{10 + x}$.

(b) Horizontal asymptote $C = 1$ (100%): adding more and more acid brings the mixture closer to pure acid but never exactly 100%.

(c) $\dfrac{ {{p0/10}} + x}{10 + x} = {{T/100}}$: ${{p0/10}} + x = {{T/10}} + {{T/100}}x$, so ${{1-T/100}}x = {{T/10-p0/10}}$ and $x = {{(T/10-p0/10)/(1-T/100):3}}$ L.

rubric.point: Sets up and solves the equation

questions.text: For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + {{b}}}{x - {{d}}}$, calculate $f({{d}}.01)$ and $f({{d-1}}.99)$ and use them to describe the behaviour of the function near its vertical asymptote.

Design two different rational functions of the form $f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}$ that both have vertical asymptote $x = {{q}}$ and horizontal asymptote $y = {{r}}$, but different $x$-intercepts. Give the intercepts of each and explain what is the same and what is different about the graphs.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any function $\dfrac{ {{r}}x + b}{x - {{q}}}$ works (with $b \ne -{{r*q}}$, otherwise there is a hole).

Example 1: $f(x) = \dfrac{ {{r}}x + {{r}} }{x - {{q}}}$: $x$-intercept $-1$, $y$-intercept $-\frac{ {{r}} }{ {{q}} } \approx {{-r/q:3}}$.

Example 2: $g(x) = \dfrac{ {{r}}x - {{r*(q+2)}} }{x - {{q}}}$: $x$-intercept {{q+2}}, $y$-intercept $\frac{ {{r*(q+2)}} }{ {{q}} } \approx {{r*(q+2)/q:3}}$.

Same: asymptotes, domain $x \ne {{q}}$, range $y \ne {{r}}$, centre of symmetry $({{q}}, {{r}})$. Different: intercepts and the stretch about the asymptotes; also the branches of $g$ lie in the opposite pair of regions from $f$ (in $g$ the numerator constant makes $k = b + {{r*q}}$ negative), so $g$ increases on each branch while $f$ decreases.

rubric.point: Two valid functions with the given asymptotes
Avoids the hole case or explains it
